extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers interested in natural history and popular science (readers of Popular Science Monthly / Macmillan's Magazine)
extracted.subtask_description: Magazine-length biographical sketch / obituary of a naturalist intended to inform and entertain a general readership; combines life-history, anecdotes, evaluation of work, and reflections on the author's field. Emphasizes popular-science prose and public-facing qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make natural history practical and popular
rubrics_metrics.description: It was his object ... to make natural history practical; but it was his real mission to make natural history and fish-culture popular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid obscure scientific terminology; use plain language so topics become accessible to thousands of households. Evidence: Buckland 'hated the scientific terms which other naturalists employed, and invariably used the simplest language for describing his meaning.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use humor and provoke laughter in popular science writing and lectures
rubrics_metrics.description: He remembered his father's lectures, and always thought it his first duty to make his audience laugh; and he had a dozen stories ready to provoke laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ anecdotes, light-hearted jokes, and comic incidents to engage broad audiences both in print and in public lectures. Examples: amusing railway/ticket anecdotes, practical jokes with specimens, comic classroom/lecture habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciliatory public-speaking / audience management
rubrics_metrics.description: If a close observer were asked to mention the chief quality which Mr. Buckland developed as Inspector of Fisheries, he would probably reply, a capacity for managing men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be genial and approachable to thaw reserve and elicit information; conciliatory manner converts suspicious or hostile listeners into cooperative informants. Use warmth and wit to win over both less-educated and more-educated audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energetic, hands-on field zeal and practical inspection
rubrics_metrics.description: No public officer ever threw himself so heartily into his work ... He has been known to wade up to his neck in water, and change his clothes driving away from the river on the box of a fly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective fieldwork requires physical endurance, willingness to endure discomfort, direct inspection, and active specimen collection. Practical enthusiasm can produce thorough results (e.g., turning over coffins in search of Hunter's remains; collecting thousands of specimens).

rubrics_metrics.name: Train the eye to observe and amass collections to illustrate science
rubrics_metrics.description: He had trained himself to observe, and his eye rarely missed anything ... One of Mr. Buckland's main objects was to form a collection which would illustrate the whole science of fish-culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic observation and maintaining illustrative collections/museums are central to scientific popularization and pedagogy; a well-curated collection can further public engagement and instruction (as at South Kensington).

rubrics_metrics.name: Traits contributing to a successful/popular naturalist
rubrics_metrics.description: Kindliness, genial humour, energy, industry, and simplicity of manner were central to his success; he rarely said a hard word and could not resist a cry of distress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal qualities — generosity, simplicity, vivacity, and approachability — help secure public affection and effectiveness in public roles; these traits complement technical competence and support long-term influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions of felicity for naturalists (what makes a naturalist happy)
rubrics_metrics.description: A pursuit which strongly interests you; the naturalist has his pursuit, which never tires him, never fails him, and can never come to an end. ... No man ever hopes to know [it] all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Happiness and sustained engagement derive from an inexhaustible subject, continual results (even negative ones), and the possibility of making a living from an engrossing pursuit. This is presented as a normative account of what makes the vocation rewarding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular-writing economy and spontaneity
rubrics_metrics.description: His best things, he used to say himself, were written on the box of an omnibus or in a railway-carriage. 'The Royal Academy without a Catalogue' was written between London and Crewe, and posted at the latter station.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short, spontaneous pieces produced in transit can have high quality for popular audiences; overlaboured compositions may lose the lively traits that appeal to readers. Favor concise, immediate prose when writing for general-interest magazines.
